abstract: Grasslands are facing unprecedented habitat loss due to settler-driven agriculture during colonial expansion, conversion to tree plantations, misclassification as wastelands, absorption into megadevelopment projects, and insufficient response to climate change. Globally, grassland birds have faced the steepest declines, with many formerly common species facing rapid decline, losing much of their original ranges. In South Asia, our knowledge of how these land-use changes in grasslands have affected birds remain scant. Natural history collections and archives are vital resources to identify historical baselines for conducting a resurvey and identifying trends in long-term biodiversity response. Yet such historical data remain insufficient in tropical regions. In this study, by compiling an unprecedented dataset of ornithological surveys from the 1900s using a diverse set of historical data, we conducted a 3-year resurvey in an Eastern Himalayan grassland first surveyed by British Ornithologist Herbert Stevens. We surveyed nine historical localities. Using a recently developed Bayesian method to calibrate modern surveys with historical museum data, we found a 70.5% decline in grassland specialist birds. We also report the local extirpation of four endemic species of grassland birds. Open habitat raptors showed a 74.9% decline, while generalist species showed an increase of 23.5% and wetland birds showed a marginal increase of 2.64%. By quantifying functional distinctiveness, a measure of morphological diversity, we find that loss of grassland species does not impact morphological and functional diversity in modern assemblage. We also find that most resurvey localities have a high number of invasive species that have completely altered these communities. Grassland specialist birds of South Asia are highly range-restricted and have specific habitat requirements; the lack of intact tall grass communities in concert with site-level disturbance pressures from grazing, conversion and fire have likely contributed to their local extirpation. Our study serves as one of the first efforts to resurvey wet grasslands of South Asia and document local-level extirpation. We also highlight the importance of museum-based research to document long-term changes for urgent conservation attention.
